subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: Sahil, you are captain this year, so hear how Deepak did it at fifteen. Our school was planning Sports Day and I had a list as long as my arm and no idea who should do what. I would have painted the posters myself, badly. Then I thought: who in my class writes like a printed book? Nusrat. And who knows every shopkeeper on the road and could get the permission letters signed at the ward office? Gopal. I did not pick names out of a hat. I went to Nusrat and said, "Your writing is the best in our class, will you do the posters?" Then to Gopal: "You know people, can you get the permissions?" Both said yes at once, because I had named what they were good at. I kept the sports list for myself.

qa.q: Who was asked to do the posters?
qa.a: Nusrat was asked to do the posters.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel at the start, holding a list as long as an arm?
qa.a: Deepak felt overwhelmed and unsure who should do what.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made both classmates say yes, and why?
qa.a: Deepak named what each classmate was good at, so the request felt like a recognition of a real skill.

qa.q: How might Gopal have felt when asked about the permissions?
qa.a: Gopal may have felt pleased and trusted, since the request showed that Deepak had noticed the skill.

grounding: Shows a student captain choosing a poster maker and a permissions person by what each is good at.

subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: Two days before the inter-house quiz, the hall still wasn't booked and the corridor had no posters. Pradeep, the house captain, sat on the stairs with his list and talked it through under his breath. "If I do the posters, they'll look like a spider walked through ink. Samir's notebook headings are neater than printed ones, so posters are his." He crossed out his own name. "The hall slip is harder. I go blank in front of the office clerks. But the vice-captain runs errands there every lunch break and knows everyone by name. They'll say yes to a familiar face." He texted both of them before the bell. By Thursday afternoon Samir had three bright posters on the notice board, and the vice-captain came back waving a signed slip. The hall was theirs for Friday.

qa.q: Why did Pradeep give the posters to Samir?
qa.a: Because Samir's notebook headings are neater than printed ones.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling about going to the office himself?
qa.a: Pradeep felt nervous about it; he says he goes blank in front of the office clerks, which is part of why he hands the slip to someone at ease there.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep have tried if nobody on the team knew the office staff?
qa.a: He could ask the teacher in charge of the quiz to introduce them, or take a short written request so his nerves matter less.

qa.q: How might Samir see being picked for the posters?
qa.a: Samir would likely feel pleased and trusted, because he was chosen for a skill he actually has rather than handed a random job.

grounding: A teen captain, short on time, reasons aloud about who suits each job: neat lettering for posters, familiarity with the office for the permission.

subtype: Approach: assigns jobs by each person's strengths [Thinking]
passage: On the metro home, Dilnaz scrolled through the class group and talked her plan out loud to Divyansh. "The book swap needs posters by Monday and a yes for the courtyard. I was going to split jobs alphabetically, but that's silly." She tapped the screen. "The boy who does calligraphy for the school magazine: his letters are gorgeous, so posters go to him. And you." She pointed at Divyansh. "You're on first-name terms with half the office because of debate club. You ask for the courtyard." Divyansh grinned. "So I'm the talker?" "You're the one they'll say yes to. If I send someone they've never met, it waits a week." He agreed before their station. On Monday the posters went up, and the courtyard was booked for Saturday morning.

qa.q: What event is Dilnaz's class planning?
qa.a: A book swap, which needs posters by Monday and a yes for the courtyard.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz drop her first idea of splitting jobs alphabetically?
qa.a: She realised it was silly and felt uneasy about the delay a stranger might face; matching jobs to what people are good at felt more sensible and hopeful.

qa.q: Which other approach could work if Divyansh were busy with exams?
qa.a: Dilnaz could go with a teacher who knows the office, or ask Divyansh for a quick introduction so the request still comes through a familiar face.

qa.q: How does Divyansh see being chosen as 'the talker'?
qa.a: He seems amused and a little flattered that his debate-club friendships are useful, and he agrees quickly.

grounding: A student captain explains aloud why the calligraphy student gets the posters and the well-connected classmate gets the permission.
